units.title: Color contrast
units.learn: Color contrast refers to the difference in brightness between the foreground (text) and the background. This matters because if the contrast is too low, people with low vision, color blindness, or even someone using a phone in bright sunlight won't be able to read your content. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) provide specific ratios to aim for (e.g., 4.5:1 for normal text). A short code example: `.text { color: #555; background: #fff; /* Ratio is 7.46:1 - Good! */ }`. A common beginner mistake is using light gray text on a white background because it looks "modern" or "minimalist," but this is one of the most common accessibility failures on the web.

units.title: Screen reader text
units.learn: Screen reader text is content that is meant specifically for users of assistive technology and is hidden from sighted users. This matters because sometimes a visual design uses icons or layout to convey meaning that isn't present in the text alone. For example, a "Trash" icon button needs the words "Delete item" for someone who can't see the icon. A short code example: ``. A common beginner mistake is using `display: none;` or `visibility: hidden;` to hide this text; these properties hide the content from *everyone*, including screen readers. Instead, you must use a special "visually-hidden" CSS class that keeps the text in the document but shrinks it to 1px.

units.title: Accessible form flow
units.learn: Accessible form flow is the logical and predictable sequence of steps a user takes to complete a form. This matters because if a form's structure is confusing or the focus jumps around randomly, users (especially those using screen readers or keyboards) will get lost or give up. A good flow follows the visual order of the page, provides clear error feedback, and returns the user to the right place after a mistake. A short code example: `<form> <!-- 1. Personal Info --> <fieldset>...</fieldset> <!-- 2. Payment --> <fieldset>...</fieldset> <button type="submit">Complete Purchase</button> </form>`. A common beginner mistake is using JavaScript to move the focus to a new part of the page without warning, which can be disorienting for users who can't see the whole screen.

units.title: Class naming
units.learn: Class naming is the practice of giving meaningful and consistent names to your CSS classes. This matters because as a project grows, vague names like `.box1` or `.blue-text` become impossible to manage. Good class names describe *what* an element is or *what* its purpose is, rather than how it looks. A short code example: `/* Bad */ .red-box { color: red; } /* Good */ .alert-message { color: red; }`. This allows you to change the color later without the class name becoming a lie. A common beginner mistake is using names that are too specific to the current design (like `.left-sidebar`) which breaks if the layout changes. Instead, use names that describe the content or component.

units.title: Component CSS
units.learn: Component CSS is the philosophy of writing styles that are encapsulated within specific UI "components" (like a card, a button, or a navbar). This matters because it prevents "style leakage," where a style for one part of the page accidentally breaks another. Instead of writing one giant CSS file, you think in terms of independent, reusable blocks. A short code example: `.user-profile { border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 10px; } .user-profile__avatar { border-radius: 50%; }`. A common beginner mistake is writing overly broad selectors like `div p { ... }` which affects every paragraph in every div. By using component-specific classes, you ensure that your styles are predictable and easy to move around.

units.learn:
Utility CSS (also called Functional or Atomic CSS) is an approach where you use small, single-purpose classes to build your UI directly in the HTML. This matters because it allows for extremely rapid development and ensures a very consistent design system. Instead of writing a new `.card` class, you combine utilities like `.p-4` (padding), `.bg-white` (background), and `.rounded` (border-radius). A short code example: `

units.title: CSS modules
units.learn: CSS Modules are a build-time solution that makes your CSS classes "local" by default. This matters because in traditional CSS, every class is global; if you have a `.title` class in two different files, they will conflict. CSS Modules solve this by automatically renaming your classes to something unique (like `.title_abc123`) during the build process. A short code example: `/* Button.module.css */ .btn { color: blue; }` and in JS: `import styles from './Button.module.css'; <button className={styles.btn}>`. A common beginner mistake is trying to use a CSS Module class name as a plain string (like `className="btn"`); because the class name was changed by the build tool, the plain string won't match anything.

units.title: Cascade layers
units.learn: Cascade layers (`@layer`) are a modern CSS feature that gives you explicit control over the "cascade" (the order in which styles are applied). This matters because it solves the "specificity wars" where you have to use `!important` or deeply nested selectors to override styles. By putting CSS into layers, you decide which layer "wins," regardless of the specificity of the selectors inside them. A short code example: `@layer base, components, utilities; @layer base { h1 { color: gray; } } @layer utilities { .red { color: red; } }`. In this example, the `utilities` layer always wins over the `base` layer. A common beginner mistake is thinking that a more specific selector in a lower layer will beat a simple selector in a higher layer; with layers, the layer order is the ultimate authority.

units.title: Design tokens
units.learn: Design tokens are the "atomic" values of a design system, such as specific colors, spacing units, and font sizes, stored as data (usually CSS variables). This matters because it ensures that your design stays consistent across a whole project and makes it incredibly easy to update. Instead of remembering a hex code like `#3b82f6`, you use a token like `--color-primary`. A short code example: `:root { --spacing-md: 1rem; --color-brand: #ff0000; } .card { padding: var(--spacing-md); color: var(--color-brand); }`. A common beginner mistake is hard-coding values directly in components; when the "brand red" changes slightly, you have to find and replace it in 50 different files. With design tokens, you change it once in the `:root` and the whole site updates instantly.

units.title: Theming
units.learn: Theming is the ability to change the entire visual look of a website (colors, fonts, etc.) by switching a set of values. This matters because it allows for features like "Dark Mode," "High Contrast Mode," or even multi-brand websites that share the same code but look different. In modern CSS, theming is best achieved using CSS Variables. You define your theme values at the top level and use them throughout your components. A short code example: `:root { --bg: white; --text: black; } [data-theme='dark'] { --bg: black; --text: white; } body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }`. A common beginner mistake is creating entirely separate CSS files for different themes, which leads to massive code duplication. By using variables, you only change the "data" while the layout logic stays the same.

units.title: Dark mode
units.learn: Dark mode is a specific theme that uses light-colored text on a dark background. This matters because it reduces eye strain in low-light environments, saves battery on OLED screens, and is a highly requested feature by users. In CSS, you implement it using the `prefers-color-scheme` media query or by toggling a class with JavaScript. A short code example: `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { --bg: #121212; --text: #ffffff; } }`. A common beginner mistake is using pure black (`#000000`) for the background and pure white (`#ffffff`) for the text; this can create too much contrast and cause "haloing" or eye fatigue. Instead, use dark grays and slightly off-white colors for a more comfortable experience.

units.title: Print styles
units.learn: Print styles are a set of CSS rules that apply only when a user prints a web page. This matters because websites are designed for screens (wide, glowing, interactive), but paper is static, narrow, and expensive (ink!). Good print styles ensure that your content is readable and doesn't waste resources. You implement this using the `@media print` query. A short code example: `@media print { .navbar, .ads { display: none; } body { font-size: 12pt; color: black; } }`. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to hide interactive elements like navigation menus, videos, or "Submit" buttons, which are useless on a piece of paper.

units.title: Style quality checks
units.learn: Style quality checks are the process of reviewing your CSS to ensure it is clean, efficient, and bug-free. This matters because messy CSS leads to "technical debt," making it harder and more expensive to fix things later. Quality checks involve using tools like "Linters" to find errors, checking for unused CSS, and ensuring your code follows a consistent style guide. A short code example: `/* Bad */ .box{color:red;margin:10px} /* Good - consistent spacing */ .box { color: red; margin: 10px; }`. A common beginner mistake is ignoring browser warnings in the DevTools or having duplicate CSS rules that cancel each other out. By performing regular quality checks, you keep your website fast and your codebase healthy.

units.title: Landing page
units.learn: A landing page is a standalone web page created specifically for a marketing or advertising campaign. It's where a visitor "lands" after clicking on a link in an email, or ads from Google, Bing, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, or similar places on the web. Unlike other pages on your website, which typically have many goals and encourage exploration, landing pages are designed with a single focus or goal, known as a Call to Action (CTA). This simplicity is what makes landing pages the best option for increasing the conversion rates of your marketing campaigns and lowering your cost of acquiring a lead or sale. In terms of CSS, a landing page often requires a strong visual hierarchy, clear typography, and a responsive layout that looks great on all devices. Common elements include a hero section with a compelling headline, a description of the offer, social proof (like testimonials or logos), and a prominent CTA button.

units.title: Responsive navigation
units.learn: Responsive navigation is a critical component of modern web design, ensuring that users can easily navigate a website regardless of their device's screen size. On large screens, navigation is typically displayed as a horizontal bar with links spread out. However, on smaller screens like smartphones, this horizontal layout becomes impractical. A common solution is to transform the navigation into a "hamburger menu" — a small icon (usually three horizontal lines) that, when clicked, reveals a vertical list of links. Implementing this requires a combination of CSS media queries to change the layout and often a bit of JavaScript to handle the menu's open/close state. A common beginner mistake is making navigation links too small or too close together on mobile, making them difficult to tap. Using Flexbox for the horizontal layout and then switching to a column-based layout with larger touch targets for mobile is a best practice. Ensuring that the navigation remains accessible, for example by using proper ARIA labels for the menu button, is also essential.

units.title: Pricing section
units.learn: A pricing section is a crucial part of any product or service-oriented website, clearly presenting different tiers or plans to potential customers. A well-designed pricing section uses a clear visual hierarchy to help users compare features and prices quickly. This often involves using "pricing cards" — distinct containers for each plan. To make one plan stand out (like a "most popular" or "pro" plan), designers often use subtle visual cues like a different background color, a "popular" badge, or a slightly larger size. From a CSS perspective, Flexbox or Grid are excellent for creating the horizontal layout of these cards on desktop and then stacking them vertically on mobile. A common beginner mistake is making the pricing section too cluttered or not providing enough contrast between the plans, making it difficult for users to make a decision. Using consistent spacing, clear typography, and a prominent CTA button for each plan is essential for a high-converting pricing section.

units.title: Profile card
units.learn: A profile card is a common UI component used to display a summary of information about a person, such as their name, photo, job title, and social media links. It's often used in "About Us" pages, team directories, or user profiles. A well-designed profile card is visually appealing and presents the most important information clearly. From a CSS perspective, a profile card typically involves a container with a background color or shadow, a circular or rounded image, and styled text for the name and title. Flexbox is often used to align the elements within the card, such as centering the image and text. A common beginner mistake is not properly sizing the profile image or not providing enough contrast between the text and the background. Using `border-radius: 50%;` is a classic technique for creating circular profile photos. Ensuring the card is responsive and looks good on different screen sizes is also important, perhaps by adjusting its width or the layout of its internal elements.

units.title: Settings form
units.learn: A settings form is a common UI pattern that allows users to view and modify their account information, preferences, or application configurations. These forms can range from simple (e.g., changing a username) to complex (e.g., managing privacy, notifications, and security settings). A well-designed settings form is organized, easy to navigate, and provides clear feedback to the user. From a CSS perspective, this involves using consistent spacing between form fields, clear labels, and well-styled input elements. Grouping related settings into sections with headings helps users find what they're looking for. Using Flexbox or Grid can help align labels and inputs precisely. A common beginner mistake is not providing enough space between fields, making the form feel cramped and overwhelming. Ensuring that the form is accessible, for example by using proper `<label>` elements for all inputs and providing clear error messages, is also crucial. Responsive design is important to ensure the form is easy to use on both desktop and mobile devices.

units.title: Accessible modal
units.learn: A modal (or modal dialog) is a UI element that appears on top of the main page content, requiring user interaction before they can return to the rest of the application. While common for alerts, confirmations, or forms, modals can be a significant accessibility challenge if not implemented correctly. An accessible modal must be navigable by keyboard, have its focus managed (the focus should move into the modal when it opens and return to the triggering element when it closes), and be properly identified to screen readers using ARIA roles and labels (`role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, `aria-labelledby`). From a CSS perspective, a modal typically involves an "overlay" that covers the background and a "modal container" for the content. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to handle the "focus trap" — ensuring that keyboard users can't accidentally tab out of the modal and into the background content while the modal is open. Providing a clear and easily accessible "Close" button is also essential.

units.title: Animated feedback
units.learn: Animated feedback involves using subtle animations to provide visual confirmation of a user's action. This can include a button slightly changing color or "lifting" when hovered, a loading spinner appearing after a form is submitted, or a success message gently fading in. These animations matter because they make a website feel more responsive, interactive, and user-friendly. They bridge the gap between a user's action and the system's response, reducing uncertainty. From a CSS perspective, this is achieved using `transitions` for simple state changes and `animations` with `@keyframes` for more complex, multi-step movements. A common beginner mistake is making animations too long, too fast, or too distracting, which can frustrate users rather than help them. Best practices include keeping animations short (usually under 300ms), using subtle effects, and ensuring they don't interfere with the user's primary task.

units.title: Browser testing
units.learn: Browser testing is the process of ensuring that your website looks and functions correctly across different web browsers (like Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge) and various devices and operating systems. This is necessary because different browsers can sometimes interpret CSS and HTML in slightly different ways, leading to unexpected layout issues or broken features. Testing involves manually checking your site in different browsers, using browser developer tools to simulate different screen sizes, and sometimes using automated tools for broader coverage. A common beginner mistake is only testing in their own favorite browser and assuming it will look the same for everyone else. Best practices include testing early and often, focusing on the most popular browsers used by your target audience, and using tools like BrowserStack or simply the built-in responsive mode in your browser's dev tools to identify and fix cross-browser inconsistencies.

units.title: Performance pass
units.learn: A performance pass is a dedicated phase in web development focused on optimizing a website's loading speed and overall responsiveness. This is critical because slow-loading sites frustrate users, increase bounce rates, and can negatively impact search engine rankings. A performance pass involves several techniques: optimizing images (reducing file size without losing quality), minifying CSS and JavaScript (removing unnecessary characters like spaces and comments), reducing the number of HTTP requests (e.g., by combining files), and leveraging browser caching. From a CSS perspective, this also includes avoiding overly complex selectors and minimizing the use of large, unoptimized web fonts. A common beginner mistake is ignoring performance until the very end or using massive, uncompressed images that slow down the page significantly. Best practices include using tools like Google PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse to identify performance bottlenecks and focusing on the "Critical Rendering Path" to get the most important content to the user as quickly as possible.

units.title: Final interface project
units.learn: The final interface project is the culmination of everything you've learned in this HTML/CSS course. It's an opportunity to apply all the concepts — from basic syntax and the box model to advanced Flexbox, Grid, responsive design, and accessibility — to build a complete, professional-looking web interface. This project typically involves taking a design (either your own or a provided mockup) and translating it into clean, semantic HTML and well-organized, efficient CSS. It's not just about making it look good; it's about making it functional, responsive, and accessible to all users. A common beginner mistake is rushing the process or neglecting the small details that make a big difference, like consistent spacing, clear typography, and thoughtful interactive states. Best practices include planning your layout first, using a mobile-first approach, writing modular and reusable CSS, and thoroughly testing your interface in different browsers and on various devices. This project is a chance to showcase your skills and create a piece for your portfolio that demonstrates your proficiency in modern web styling.
